solution:
True. When a helical coil is pulled at its ends, the wire of which the coil is made is not appreciably stretched along its own length. Instead every small element of the wire is twisted about the wire's own axis, and a twist is a shear deformation — adjacent layers of the wire slide over one another while the wire's length and volume stay essentially unchanged.

The extension of the coil is therefore set by how easily the wire shears, i.e. by the shear modulus \(G\) of its material, and not by its Young's modulus \(Y\) (which would govern a straight wire of the same material pulled along its length).

True.

The load hangs from a face parallel to the applied force, so the cube is sheared, not stretched.

Edge \(L = 10\,\text{cm} = 0.10\,\text{m}\), so the sheared face has area \(A = L^{2} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}^{2}\).

Tangential force \(F = mg = 100 \times 9.8 = 980\,\text{N}\).

Shear stress \(= \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{980}{1.0 \times 10^{-2}} = 9.8 \times 10^{4}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\).

Shear strain \(\theta = \dfrac{\text{shear stress}}{G} = \dfrac{9.8 \times 10^{4}}{25 \times 10^{9}} = 3.92 \times 10^{-6}\).

The vertical deflection of the loaded face is \(\Delta L = \theta L = 3.92 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.10\).

Vertical deflection \(\Delta L = 3.92 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\)

The load is shared equally, so each column carries one quarter of the weight:

\(F = \dfrac{Mg}{4} = \dfrac{50000 \times 9.8}{4} = \dfrac{4.9 \times 10^{5}}{4} = 1.225 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N}\).

Each column is hollow, so only the annular cross-section carries the load. With \(R = 60\,\text{cm} = 0.60\,\text{m}\) and \(r = 30\,\text{cm} = 0.30\,\text{m}\),

\(A = \pi (R^{2} - r^{2}) = \pi (0.36 - 0.09) = 0.27\pi = 0.848\,\text{m}^{2}\).

Compressional stress \(= \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{1.225 \times 10^{5}}{0.848} = 1.444 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\).

Taking Young's modulus of mild steel \(Y = 2.0 \times 10^{11}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\),

\(\text{strain} = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{Y} = \dfrac{1.444 \times 10^{5}}{2.0 \times 10^{11}}\).

Compressional strain of each column \(= 7.22 \times 10^{-7}\) (dimensionless)

Volume strain: \(\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = \dfrac{100.5 - 100.0}{100.0} = \dfrac{0.5}{100.0} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\).

Pressure increase: \(\Delta p = 100.0 \times 1.013 \times 10^{5} = 1.013 \times 10^{7}\,\text{Pa}\).

\(B_{\text{water}} = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta V / V} = \dfrac{1.013 \times 10^{7}}{5.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 2.026 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\).

For air at constant temperature, \(pV = \text{constant}\), so \(p\,\Delta V + V\,\Delta p = 0\) and \(B_{\text{air}} = -\dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta V / V} = p \approx 1.0 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\) at atmospheric pressure.

\(\dfrac{B_{\text{water}}}{B_{\text{air}}} = \dfrac{2.026 \times 10^{9}}{1.0 \times 10^{5}} \approx 2.0 \times 10^{4}\).

Why the ratio is so large: in air the molecules are far apart compared with their own size and exert almost no force on one another, so a modest pressure simply pushes them closer together and the volume falls sharply. In water the molecules are already packed nearly in contact, and squeezing them further means working against strong short-range intermolecular repulsion. A far greater pressure is therefore needed to produce the same fractional change in volume, which is exactly what a large bulk modulus means.

\(B_{\text{water}} = 2.026 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\), and \(B_{\text{water}} / B_{\text{air}} \approx 2.0 \times 10^{4}\)

Let \(\rho = 1.03 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\) be the density at the surface and \(\rho'\) the density at depth. Take the bulk modulus of water \(B = 2.2 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\).

Pressure increase: \(\Delta p = 80.0\,\text{atm} = 80.0 \times 1.013 \times 10^{5} = 8.104 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Pa}\).

Fractional decrease in volume:

\(\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = \dfrac{\Delta p}{B} = \dfrac{8.104 \times 10^{6}}{2.2 \times 10^{9}} = 3.68 \times 10^{-3}\).

The mass of the sample is unchanged, so \(\rho' V' = \rho V\) with \(V' = V - \Delta V\):

\(\rho' = \dfrac{\rho}{1 - \Delta V / V} = \dfrac{1.03 \times 10^{3}}{1 - 3.68 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{1030}{0.99632}\).

Density at that depth \(\rho' = 1.034 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\)
_note: The stem prints the surface density as '1.03 x 103 kg m^-3' — the exponent of ten has dropped to the baseline in the source (a typesetting fault; the neighbouring 8.12 and 8.15 print their powers correctly). Solved with the physically intended value 1.03 x 10^3 kg m^-3, which is the density of sea water. Also note the answer is insensitive to whether the excess pressure is taken as 80 atm or as 80 - 1 = 79 atm above the surface: both give 1.034 x 10^3 kg m^-3 to 4 significant figures.

solution:
Hydraulic (all-round) pressure produces a volume strain governed by the bulk modulus.

\(\Delta p = 10 \times 1.013 \times 10^{5} = 1.013 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Pa}\).

Taking the bulk modulus of glass \(B = 37 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\),

\(\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = \dfrac{\Delta p}{B} = \dfrac{1.013 \times 10^{6}}{37 \times 10^{9}}\).

Fractional change in volume \(\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = 2.7 \times 10^{-5}\) (a contraction)

Edge \(L = 10\,\text{cm} = 0.10\,\text{m}\), so the original volume is

\(V = L^{3} = (0.10)^{3} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^{3}\).

Taking the bulk modulus of copper \(B = 140 \times 10^{9} = 1.4 \times 10^{11}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\), and using \(B = \dfrac{p}{\Delta V / V}\),

\(\Delta V = \dfrac{pV}{B} = \dfrac{(7.0 \times 10^{6})(1.0 \times 10^{-3})}{1.4 \times 10^{11}} = \dfrac{7.0 \times 10^{3}}{1.4 \times 10^{11}}\).

Volume contraction \(\Delta V = 5.0 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{m}^{3} = 0.05\,\text{cm}^{3}\)

A compression of \(0.10\%\) means a volume strain

\(\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = \dfrac{0.10}{100} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\).

Taking the bulk modulus of water \(B = 2.2 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\),

\(\Delta p = B \times \dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = (2.2 \times 10^{9})(1.0 \times 10^{-3})\).

Note the answer does not depend on the stated volume of one litre: the required pressure is fixed by the fractional compression alone.

In atmospheres, \(\Delta p = \dfrac{2.2 \times 10^{6}}{1.013 \times 10^{5}} \approx 21.7\,\text{atm}\).

Required pressure change \(\Delta p = 2.2 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Pa}\) (about \(21.7\,\text{atm}\))
